# Pack authoring guide, version 5

This is for mutation testing, the software testing technique that measures
how well a project's own test suite detects small deliberate changes to its
code. Each changed copy is run only against that project's tests in an
isolated checkout and is then discarded; nothing is deployed or executed
elsewhere. The tool that makes the changes is called the mutation engine.

The mutation engine reads one small JSON data pack per programming language.
The engine itself knows no language. It parses source files with the
tree-sitter grammar that ast-grep ships for the language, finds syntax nodes
the pack names, and rewrites them with the templates the pack gives. You
write the pack for one language. You are given packs for other languages as
examples of the format, not as content to copy: node kind names differ
between grammars.

## How the engine applies a pack

Knowing this helps you pick values whose output compiles and matches what is
expected.

- A statement that is dropped is replaced as a whole. The replaced text is
  the full statement wrapper node, including its terminator if the grammar
  places the terminator inside that node. The `noop_statement` text is
  inserted unchanged in its place; the engine adds nothing around it.
- A failure rewrite replaces only the text of the failure node itself with
  the filled-in template. Everything around the node stays as it was.
- A site is changed only if its node kind appears in the pack. Two packs
  that list the same sites but produce different text at them count as
  different packs, so the exact text of `noop_statement` and of every
  template matters as much as the kind names.

## Fields

All node kind names must be exact node type names of the tree-sitter grammar
for the target language. A name that does not exist in the grammar makes the
whole pack invalid.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `language` | The language name as ast-grep spells it, lower case |
| `comment_kinds` | Node kinds of comments. Nothing inside them is ever touched |
| `string_kinds` | Node kinds of string literals, including multi-part or template strings. Nothing inside them is ever touched |
| `unwrap_kinds` | Node kinds of a parenthesis wrapper that belongs to a statement's syntax, as in `if (x)`. When a condition is such a wrapper, the engine works on the expression inside it. Empty when conditions are not wrapped |
| `test_attribute_markers` | Text fragments of attributes or annotations that mark test-only code inside a production file. Empty when the language keeps tests in separate files |
| `test_attribute_kinds` | Node kinds of the attribute or annotation items that can carry one of the `test_attribute_markers`. Required when `test_attribute_markers` is not empty; leave it out otherwise |
| `kinds.branch_condition.field_of` | Pairs `[statement kind, field name]`: the named field of that statement kind holds a condition that decides control flow. List the conditional and loop statements and conditional expressions whose grammar rule has such a field |
| `kinds.branch_condition.returned` | `{"of", "kinds", "tokens"}`: `of` lists the node kinds of a return; `kinds` the node kinds of logical, comparison and negation expressions; `tokens` the operator tokens that make such an expression a yes-or-no value. A returned expression of one of these kinds with one of these operators is a condition |
| `kinds.failure_state.nodes` | Node kinds that signal failure to the caller: raising or throwing, returning, propagating an error |
| `kinds.failure_state.nodes_with_prefix` | Optional. Node kind mapped to text prefixes, for failure signals that are ordinary calls or macros in this language and can only be told apart by how they begin |
| `kinds.error_order.nodes` | The node kind of a conditional statement that can directly follow another one of the same kind. Always with `"requires_next_sibling": true` |
| `kinds.state_write.nodes` | Node kinds of assignments and in-place updates |
| `kinds.state_write.call_statements` | Node kinds of a call, and of an awaited call where the language has one, that can stand alone as a statement. Such a statement counts as a write made through a call |
| `kinds.pure_shell_boundary.nodes` | Node kinds of function and method definitions |
| `noop_statement` | Text of a statement that does nothing and is valid wherever a statement may stand |
| `statement_wrappers` | Node kinds that wrap an expression to make it a statement of its own |
| `statement_terminator` | The token that ends a simple statement, if the language has one; leave it out otherwise |

## Operators

`operators` tells the engine how to rewrite a site. Templates may use
`{text}` (the node's text), `{noop}` (the `noop_statement`) and `{child0}`
(the text of the node's first named child).

| Entry | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `operators.branch_condition.template` | Replaces a condition by its logical negation. The result must be valid syntax in the place where the condition stood, for any condition expression |
| `operators.branch_condition.token_swaps` | Pairs of operator tokens that can replace each other without changing the type of the expression: equal and not equal, a strict and a non-strict comparison, logical and and or. Spell them exactly as the language does |
| `operators.branch_condition.negation_swaps` | The pairs among `token_swaps` whose swap gives exactly the logical negation of the comparison: equal and not equal, in every spelling the language has. The engine uses it to avoid producing the same change twice. Do not list a strict and a non-strict comparison, or and and or |
| `operators.branch_condition.exclude_kinds` | Optional. Node kinds that can appear in a condition position but cannot be negated by the template, such as a pattern-binding condition or an empty condition |
| `operators.failure_state.by_kind` | Node kind mapped to a replacement template that removes the failure. Use `{noop}` for a statement that can simply be dropped. Use `{child0}` for an operator that wraps an expression to propagate its error, so that only the wrapped expression remains. Leave out kinds for which no replacement is valid in general, such as returning a value |
| `operators.failure_state.returned_literal_swaps` | Pairs of literals that can replace each other as a returned value: the two boolean literals, and 0 and 1 |
| `operators.state_write` | Always `{"statement": "{noop}"}`: a write that is a statement of its own is replaced by the empty statement |
| `operators.error_order` | Always `{"swap_next": true}` |

## Points that are easy to miss

Check each of these against the target language before you finish.

- The no-op text must stand alone. Because the noop replaces a whole
  statement, including any terminator the statement node contains, it must
  be valid when nothing follows it before the next statement. In a language
  with a terminator, a bare value expression without its terminator is
  usually not a valid statement in the middle of a block; prefer the form
  that the grammar accepts as a complete statement on its own, such as the
  bare terminator in statement-oriented languages or an empty block in
  expression-oriented languages where a block may stand as a statement
  without a terminator. In an expression-oriented language, the noop must
  also be valid as an expression and in the last position of a block. Test
  your choice mentally in three places: between two statements, as the last
  item of a block, and in place of an expression.
- Calls inside wrappers. A call that stands as a statement may be wrapped
  by a node that awaits it or propagates its error. Ask which node is the
  direct child of the statement wrapper in each case and make sure every
  such outer kind that wraps a call is covered in `call_statements`, so that
  a statement made of a wrapped call is dropped like a plain call statement.
  Do not add kinds that never wrap a call.
- Error values built by calls. In languages where a function reports
  failure by returning a value made with a standard error constructor or
  error variant (a call that always begins with the same name), that call
  is a failure site. List the call node kind under
  `failure_state.nodes_with_prefix` with the constructor name followed by
  the opening parenthesis as prefix, alongside any panic-like or abort-like
  calls or macros of the language, each under its own node kind.
- Error propagation operators. If the language has a short operator that
  returns early with the error of the expression it wraps, its node kind
  belongs in `failure_state.nodes` and also needs a rewrite in `by_kind`:
  `{child0}` keeps the wrapped expression and drops the propagation. Make
  sure the first named child of that node really is the wrapped expression
  and not the operator token. Every failure kind for which a general
  rewrite exists must have one; a failure kind without a rewrite produces
  no change at all.
- Rewrites that must type-check. A `{noop}` rewrite for a failure kind is
  only right when the failure node always stands as a statement whose value
  is not used. If the node can also be the value of a block or an argument,
  replacing it by the noop must still give valid code in those places.
- Every form of test marker. Many languages have two forms of attribute or
  annotation: one placed in front of the item it applies to, and an inner
  form placed inside a module, file or block that applies to the enclosing
  item. List the node kinds of all forms in `test_attribute_kinds`.
  Choose `test_attribute_markers` fragments that match the text of every
  form: leave out the surrounding punctuation that differs between forms,
  and cover markers written with a path prefix (a framework's own test
  attribute) as well as the plain one.
- Expression-oriented languages. Where conditionals and loops are
  expressions rather than statements, use the grammar's expression kind
  names everywhere a statement kind is asked for, and pick a `noop_statement`
  that is valid both as a statement and as an expression.
- Only real node kinds. Verify each name against the grammar's node types,
  including the names of fields used in `field_of`. Do not guess a name by
  analogy with another grammar.

## Rules

- Be precise rather than broad: a wrong kind produces changes that do not
  parse or do not compile.
- Do not include anything specific to a particular project, library or file.
- Keep the pack small: at most 40 lines and 2,500 characters, formatted like
  the examples.

## Output

Return only the JSON object of the pack, with no text before or after it.

- The engine finds statement sites through `statement_wrappers`, the node

  expression that is the whole content of a statement wrapper.

  statement anywhere in a block, including before other statements and as
  the last item of a block.

  token in normal code, even if the language allows leaving it out in some
  positions. Leave it out only when the language has no such token.
- `{child0}` is the first named child, not the first child. Before you use
  it, check that the wrapped expression really is the first named child of
  that node kind and that nothing else, such as a label or a type, comes
  first.

## The no-op statement

When the engine drops a statement, it replaces the whole statement node,
including its terminator if it has one, with the `noop_statement` text
exactly. The engine does not add a terminator. The replacement therefore
stands directly between two other statements, as the last item of a block,
or as the only item of a block.

- Choose text that is valid in all of these places without a terminator
  after it.
- Do not choose a bare value or expression that only becomes a statement
  when a terminator follows it. Such text fails to parse once the next
  statement follows it.
- In expression-oriented languages, the usual choice is the empty block. It
  is a complete statement without a terminator and is also a valid
  expression where a value of the empty type is expected.
- In languages where a lone terminator is itself the empty statement, use
  that terminator.
- Prefer the most conventional, minimal spelling. Do not add spaces or
  extra characters.

The same text is used wherever `{noop}` appears, including in
`failure_state.by_kind`. Choose it with all of those places in mind.

## Points that are easy to miss

Check each of these against the target language before you finish.

- **Error values built by calls.** In some languages a function reports
  failure by returning a value made with a standard error constructor or
  error variant, a call that always begins with the same name. That call is
  a failure site.
  - List the call node kind under `failure_state.nodes_with_prefix`, with
    the constructor name followed by the opening parenthesis as prefix.
  - Also list any panic-like or abort-like calls or macros of the language,
    each under its own node kind.
- **Error propagation operators.** Some languages have a short operator that
  returns early with the error of the expression it wraps.
  - Put its node kind in `failure_state.nodes`.
  - Give it a rewrite in `by_kind`: `{child0}` keeps the wrapped expression
    and drops the propagation.
  - Every failure kind that has a general rewrite must get one. A failure
    kind without a rewrite produces no change at all.
- **Every form of test marker.** Many languages have two forms of attribute
  or annotation. One is placed in front of the item it applies to. The other
  is an inner form, placed inside a module, file or block, that applies to
  the enclosing item.
  - List the node kinds of all forms in `test_attribute_kinds`.
  - Choose `test_attribute_markers` fragments that match the text of every
    form. Leave out the punctuation that differs between the forms.
  - Cover markers written with a path prefix, such as a framework's own test
    attribute, as well as the plain marker.
- **Test marker precision.** A fragment matches anywhere in the attribute
  text, so a short common word also matches attributes that are not test
  markers.
  - A conditional attribute that negates the test configuration marks
    production code.
  - A feature name or a lint name can contain the word "test".
  - Code under such attributes must still be changed. Pick fragments that
    match only the real test markers.
- **Expression-oriented languages.** In these languages conditionals and
  loops are expressions rather than statements.
  - Use the grammar's expression kind names everywhere a statement kind is
    asked for.
  - Check that every `{noop}` and `{child0}` replacement still parses in each
    position the replaced node can occupy: statement, block tail, operand.
- **Only real node kinds.** Verify each name against the grammar's node
  types, including the field names used in `field_of`. Do not guess a name
  by analogy with another grammar.

## Rules

- Be precise rather than broad. A wrong kind produces changes that do not
  parse or do not compile.
- Every template must produce the same text a careful human would write for
  that change. Two packs that select the same sites but produce different
  replacement text count as different changes.
- Do not include anything specific to a particular project, library or file.
- Keep the pack small: at most 40 lines and 2,500 characters, formatted like
  the examples.

Return only the JSON object of the pack, with no text before or after it.

Leave out kinds for which no replacement is valid in general, such as returning a value |
| `operators.failure_state.returned_literal_swaps` | Pairs of literals that can replace each other as a returned value: the two boolean literals, and 0 and 1 |
| `operators.state_write` | Always `{"statement": "{noop}"}`: a write that is a statement of its own is replaced by the empty statement |
| `operators.error_order` | Always `{"swap_next": true}` |

## Points that are easy to miss

Check each of these against the target language before you finish.

- Calls standing as statements, in every wrapping. The engine looks only
  at the outermost expression of a statement to decide whether it is a
  call statement. A statement whose whole expression is a call wrapped in
  an await, in an error propagation operator, or in both, is still a call
  made for its effect, and dropping it is a meaningful change. So list in
  `call_statements` the node kind of the plain call and the node kind of
  each wrapper that can hold a call and stand alone as a statement: the
  awaited expression and the error propagation expression, where the
  language has them. Leaving a wrapper out makes such statements be
  handled differently from the reference, even though every name is valid.
- Error values built by calls. In languages where a function reports
  failure by returning a value made with a standard error constructor or
  error variant (a call that always begins with the same name), that call
  is a failure site. List the call node kind under
  `failure_state.nodes_with_prefix` with the constructor name followed by
  the opening parenthesis as prefix, alongside any panic-like or abort-like
  calls or macros of the language, each under its own node kind.
- Error propagation operators. If the language has a short operator that
  returns early with the error of the expression it wraps, its node kind
  belongs in `failure_state.nodes` and also needs a rewrite in `by_kind`:
  `{child0}` keeps the wrapped expression and drops the propagation. It
  also belongs in `call_statements` as explained above; the two uses do
  not exclude each other. Every failure kind for which a general rewrite
  exists must have one; a failure kind without a rewrite produces no
  change at all.
- Every form of test marker. Many languages have two forms of attribute or
  annotation: one placed in front of the item it applies to, and an inner
  form placed inside a module, file or block that applies to the enclosing
  item. List the node kinds of all forms in `test_attribute_kinds`.
  Choose `test_attribute_markers` fragments that match the text of every
  form: leave out the surrounding punctuation that differs between forms,
  and cover markers written with a path prefix (a framework's own test
  attribute) as well as the plain one.
- Expression-oriented languages. Where conditionals and loops are
  expressions rather than statements, use the grammar's expression kind
  names everywhere a statement kind is asked for, and pick a `noop_statement`
  that is valid both as a statement and as an expression.
- Only real node kinds. Verify each name against the grammar's node types,
  including the names of fields used in `field_of`. Do not guess a name by
  analogy with another grammar. Do not list a node kind in `field_of`
  unless that exact kind has a field of that exact name that holds a
  condition.

## Rules

- Be precise rather than broad: a wrong kind produces changes that do not
  parse or do not compile.
- Do not include anything specific to a particular project, library or file.
- Keep the pack small: at most 40 lines and 2,500 characters, formatted like
  the examples.

Return only the JSON object of the pack, with no text before or after it.

# Pack authoring guide, version 5

This is for mutation testing, the software testing technique that measures
how well a project's own test suite detects small deliberate changes to its
code. Each changed copy is run only against that project's tests in an
isolated checkout and is then discarded; nothing is deployed or executed
elsewhere. The tool that makes the changes is called the mutation engine.

The mutation engine reads one small JSON data pack per programming language.
The engine itself knows no language. It parses source files with the
tree-sitter grammar that ast-grep ships for the language, finds syntax nodes
the pack names, and rewrites them with the templates the pack gives. You
write the pack for one language. You are given packs for other languages as
examples of the format, not as content to copy: node kind names differ
between grammars.

## How the engine uses the pack

Knowing this helps you choose kinds that give the intended changes:

- A site is one node of a listed kind. The engine makes one change per
  site and operator, and each change is identified by where it is and what
  text replaces it. Two packs that touch the same sites with different
  replacement text give different changes.
- A statement whose expression is a listed write or call statement is
  dropped: it is replaced by `{noop}`.
- A failure site with a template in `by_kind` is rewritten with that
  template. The same node can therefore be both dropped (as a statement)
  and rewritten (as a failure). Both are intended; make sure each kind is
  listed in every place where it belongs, so that both happen.

## Fields

All node kind names must be exact node type names of the tree-sitter grammar
for the target language. A name that does not exist in the grammar makes the
whole pack invalid.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `language` | The language name as ast-grep spells it, lower case |
| `comment_kinds` | Node kinds of comments. Nothing inside them is ever touched |
| `string_kinds` | Node kinds of string literals, including raw, multi-part or template strings. Nothing inside them is ever touched |
| `unwrap_kinds` | Node kinds of a parenthesis wrapper that belongs to a statement's syntax, as in `if (x)`. When a condition is such a wrapper, the engine works on the expression inside it. Empty when conditions are not wrapped |
| `test_attribute_markers` | Text fragments of attributes or annotations that mark test-only code inside a production file. Empty when the language keeps tests in separate files |
| `test_attribute_kinds` | Node kinds of the attribute or annotation items that can carry one of the `test_attribute_markers`. Required when `test_attribute_markers` is not empty; leave it out otherwise |
| `kinds.branch_condition.field_of` | Pairs `[statement kind, field name]`: the named field of that statement kind holds a condition that decides control flow. List the conditional and loop statements and conditional expressions whose grammar rule has such a field |
| `kinds.branch_condition.returned` | `{"of", "kinds", "tokens"}`: `of` lists the node kinds of a return; `kinds` the node kinds of logical, comparison and negation expressions; `tokens` the operator tokens that make such an expression a yes-or-no value. A returned expression of one of these kinds with one of these operators is a condition |
| `kinds.failure_state.nodes` | Node kinds that signal failure to the caller: raising or throwing, returning, propagating an error |
| `kinds.failure_state.nodes_with_prefix` | Optional. Node kind mapped to text prefixes, for failure signals that are ordinary calls or macros in this language and can only be told apart by how they begin |
| `kinds.error_order.nodes` | The node kind of a conditional statement that can directly follow another one of the same kind. Always with `"requires_next_sibling": true` |
| `kinds.state_write.nodes` | Node kinds of assignments and in-place updates, including compound assignments |
| `kinds.state_write.call_statements` | Node kinds of every expression form that is a call and can stand alone as a statement: the plain call, a macro call where the language has macros, an awaited call, and a call wrapped in an error propagation operator. Such a statement counts as a write made through a call |
| `kinds.pure_shell_boundary.nodes` | Node kinds of function and method definitions |
| `noop_statement` | Text of a statement that does nothing and is valid wherever a statement may stand |
| `statement_wrappers` | Node kinds that wrap an expression to make it a statement of its own |
| `statement_terminator` | The token that ends a simple statement, if the language has one; leave it out otherwise |

## Operators

`operators` tells the engine how to rewrite a site. Templates may use
`{text}` (the node's text), `{noop}` (the `noop_statement`) and `{child0}`
(the text of the node's first named child).

| Entry | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `operators.branch_condition.template` | Replaces a condition by its logical negation. The result must be valid syntax in the place where the condition stood, for any condition expression |
| `operators.branch_condition.token_swaps` | Pairs of operator tokens that can replace each other without changing the type of the expression: equal and not equal, a strict and a non-strict comparison, logical and and or. Spell them exactly as the language does |
| `operators.branch_condition.negation_swaps` | The pairs among `token_swaps` whose swap gives exactly the logical negation of the comparison: equal and not equal, in every spelling the language has. Do not list a strict and a non-strict comparison, or and and or |
| `operators.branch_condition.exclude_kinds` | Optional. Node kinds that can appear in a condition position but cannot be negated by the template, such as a pattern-binding condition or an empty condition |
| `operators.failure_state.by_kind` | Node kind mapped to a replacement template that removes the failure. Use `{noop}` for a statement that can simply be dropped. Use `{child0}` for an operator that wraps an expression to propagate its error, so that only the wrapped expression remains. Leave out kinds for which no replacement is valid in general, such as returning a value |
| `operators.failure_state.returned_literal_swaps` | Pairs of literals that can replace each other as a returned value: the two boolean literals, and 0 and 1 |
| `operators.state_write` | Always `{"statement": "{noop}"}` |
| `operators.error_order` | Always `{"swap_next": true}` |

## Points that are easy to miss

Check each of these against the target language before you finish.

- Error values built by calls. Where a function reports failure by

- Error propagation operators. If the language has a short operator that

- Calls in every form. Go through the ways a call can be the whole of a

  terminator or an empty block. In expression-oriented languages pick the

  statement stands and where the last expression of a block stands.

- Expression-oriented languages. Where conditionals and loops are
  expressions, use the grammar's expression kind names everywhere a
  statement kind is asked for.
